_comment: Documented alternative conceptions for the average-speed topic, authored by the procedure in docs/misconception_library.md. Every persona for this topic is built on the first entry; the rest are recorded because the research was done. Ordering is by how well documented the conception is. Citations live in speed.sources.md. Unlike the other topics in this catalog, the strong literature here is mathematics education rather than science education, and there is no AAAS/BSCS item-bank coverage of rate or averaging, so no measured selection rates exist.
canonical_explanation: Average speed is the whole distance divided by the whole time, and because the 30 mph leg takes twice as long as the 60 mph leg, the trip averages 40 mph rather than 45.
answer_giveaway_terms: total distance divided by total time
twice as long at the slower speed
more time at the slower speed
spends longer on the slow leg

misconceptions.name: The average speed is the average of the two speeds
misconceptions.belief: Average means you add the numbers up and divide by how many there are. That is what average has always meant. So with two speeds you add them and halve it. He drove the same road both ways, so the two speeds count the same as each other. You just split the difference.
misconceptions.predicts: 45 mph. It also predicts the answer would only change if the two legs were different lengths, and that coming back at 90 instead would make it 60.
changes_only_when: you pick an actual number of miles for the trip and count up the hours each leg really took
your add-and-halve gives an answer you can see is silly and you cannot explain the silliness away
someone makes you say what your number would mean on the clock, so how long the whole trip would take if you really drove at that one speed the whole way
misconceptions.slides_into: That you cannot answer it at all because nobody said how far it is, or that you pick a distance, get the two leg times right, and then divide the total by two because there were two legs.

misconceptions.name: Average speed means the speed you were doing most of the time
misconceptions.belief: Average speed is just the speed you were mostly going at. If someone says they averaged 45 on a trip, that means the needle sat around 45 for most of the drive. It is the normal speed for that journey, the one that happened the most.
misconceptions.predicts: Either one of the two numbers you were given, because that is the speed you were mostly on, or 45 as the number the needle would sit around. Either way it is not something you work out from the trip.
changes_only_when: you have to check your answer against the clock for the whole journey instead of against what the needle looked like
you meet a trip where the speed you were on the most is nowhere near the number the question is after
someone asks what your answer would be if one leg were ten times longer than the other
misconceptions.slides_into: That you should add the two speeds and halve them, because at least that is a rule you can carry out.

misconceptions.name: Speed is a distance, so equal distances mean the speeds count equally
misconceptions.belief: Speed is basically how far you get. 60 means you are 60 ahead, 30 means you are 30 ahead. He drove the same road both ways, so the two halves of the trip are exactly the same size, which means the two speeds count exactly the same as each other.
misconceptions.predicts: 45, argued from the road being the same length each way. You reason entirely in miles and never bring hours into it; asked which leg was longer, you say neither, it is the same road.
changes_only_when: you have to describe the trip in hours instead of in miles
you watch two things moving at different speeds and see the gap between them keep growing instead of staying the same size
you are made to fill in a table with a time in it for each leg, not just a distance
misconceptions.slides_into: That speed is miles per hour after all, but that you still combine two of them by adding and halving.

misconceptions.name: Going twice as fast on the way back cancels out going slow on the way there
misconceptions.belief: He was slow one way and fast the other way, so it evens out. Whatever you lost going there you get back coming home. Double the speed on the way back cancels the slow half, so you end up dead in the middle.
misconceptions.predicts: 45, and that the answer moves in a straight line with the return speed, so coming back at 90 gives 60 and at 120 gives 75. It also predicts that driving both ways at 45 would take the same total time as the real trip did.
changes_only_when: you push the return speed to something ridiculous and your rule spits out an answer that cannot happen
you write down what actually happens to the clock when you double the speed over a fixed stretch of road
you compare this trip against one where the two legs really are different lengths and see your rule give the same kind of answer for both
misconceptions.slides_into: That the two legs are not the same after all, so you weight them, but you weight them by miles rather than by hours and land back on the same number.
